Polysyllables take primary stress on the ultima, secondary stress on the first syllable ... Within the phrase qualifying elements take primary stress, qualified elements secondary or tertiary stress: /tŋàaj níh/ 'this day = today', /jùp mɛ́ɲ/ 'last…

4402.prule: Primary (strong) stress on the final syllable of the word, whatever its length or syllable type: monosyllables in isolation are stressed; native disyllables (presyllable + main syllable) and disyllabic compounds stress the ultima; polysyllables stress the ultima. Fixed-final, quantity-insensitive.
4402.srule: Secondary (moderate, grave-marked) stress on the first syllable of polysyllables (three or more syllables; the examples are loans), primary on the ultima: /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone', /wìtsəwɔkɔ́ɔn/ 'engineer'. Disyllables (native presyllable + main syllable, and disyllabic compounds) carry the final primary only; their first syllable is unmarked (tertiary/weak).
4402.quote: There are 3 degrees of stress: primary or strong, secondary or moderate, and tertiary or weak. Primary and secondary stress are represented by the acute and grave respectively while tertiary stress is unmarked. As in the standard, monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress: /báan/ '[I] can [do it]', /srúuəl/ '[It's] easy'; dissyllables of native provenance take primary stress on the ultima: /cənnə́ər/ 'ladder', /ləmbáak/ 'trouble'. The same pattern obtains in dissyllabic compounds: /koon kóon/ 'children', /pləəw tnɔ́l/ 'road, highway'. Polysyllables take primary stress on the ulti…

4402.tone: Not tonal, no register. Smalley 1976 p. 48: 'Since Northern Khmer is not a tonal language...'; Jenner 1974 p. 62: 'Register appears to be entirely absent'. Jenner 2.2 Intonation (p. 66-67) describes 3 pitch levels and four clause-terminal contours (rising = question, sustained = suspension, circumflex = questions with /nəə/ and enclitic /qə/, falling = declarative completion), all phrase-level intonation, not lexical tone. evidence_works.detail: Author is a native speaker of the Surin variety: sec. 1.4 p. 14 'I was born in Ban Koh Tlung, Tambon Burasri, Amphoe Muang, Surin. I speak Northern Khmer as my mother tongue. So I elicited the data and described the grammatical system of the language by myself, and then checked the data with my mother-in-law, Mrs. Chaey Sujinpram, a 74-year-old woman who has lived in the area since her birth'; sec. 1.6 p. 15: the village is 'located 9 kilometers east of Surin'; sec. 1.7 Methodology p. 15: 'I collected data by myself. The data are based on my knowledge of Northern Khmer as a native speaker. Additional information is from my mother-in-law as stated in Sec.1.4 p.14.' No dedicated stress section and no explicit placement rule. What it adds to the entry: (a) foot structure, 1.10.3 p. (b) 2.2.3.2 In Unstressed Syllables: 'Unstressed syllables in Northern Khmer may often be reduced and have freely varying allomorphs'; 2.4.2 Reduction p. 52: 'the unstressed presyllables of disyllabic words are the least stable, and tend to undergo change in rapid speech', with reduction patterns 1-6 for presyllables (e.g. p. 52 /kancɒp --> kəncɒp --> kcɒp/ 'to wrap, pack'), which is the presyllable = unstressed, main syllable = stressed pattern; (c) compounds, 2.4.2 item 7 p. 54: '/pram/ "five" is subject to extreme reduction when it does not carry primary stress: /pram-mɷ:j --> prəm-mɷ:j --> pmɷ:j/ "six"' (vowel as printed, closed omega; the row quote writes mɔ:j), and 2.4.3.6 p. 66: 'Compounds are phonologically close-knit and they become one foot (one stress group); but noun phrases are not', p. 67: 'In compounds, if the first element is a long vowel it is usually reduced to a short vowel' - the compound is one stress group and its non-final element is reduced, which refines the WORD domain: compound = one stress group, noun phrase = more than one. (d) The thesis's only stress-marked compound, 3.1.3.3 Semantic Prosodies p. 194, '(a) Stress:', contrasts /'kon-proh/ (Compound Noun) 'a son' with /ko:n 'proh/ (Noun phrase) 'a male child (i.e. not a female child)' and /nsɯ: 'ɲom/ 'my book (i.e. not yours, hers, etc.)': the stress mark stands before the first element of the compound but on the final element of the emphasised phrases; whether the compound mark denotes first-element stress or the single stress group of the whole compound is not stated, so this passage is filed as a point to adjudicate rather than as agreement with Jenner's ultima statement for compounds. Symbols list p. xviii (' = stress; a curved rising arrow = stress and rising pitch), 3.2.3.3.1 p. 232 ('A stress and a rising pitch is put on the element to be emphasized'), p. 194 (a)-(d) and the clause-level remarks on pp. 248 and 337 concern emphatic phrase-level prominence, not lexical placement.

4403.prule: Fixed final, quantity-insensitive: main word stress falls on the last syllable of the word-form; when affixes are added it moves to the new final syllable (with some unspecified exceptions). Phonetic correlate: an obligatory F0 rise / pitch peak on the final syllable in every word-form type, optionally accompanied by duration and intensity (p. 84); Baskakov 1972: 38, as reported on p. 79, had the same placement ('fixed, as a rule, on the last syllable of the word') but called it expiratory.
4403.srule: None: Seljutina 1998: 80-81 raises and then refutes a hypothesised secondary, length-based stress on the initial syllable ('...что опровергает предположение о наличии в языке кумандинцев второстепенного долготного ударения на первом слоге (или на одном из первых слогов)', p. 81); initial-syllable vowel lengthening is phonemic/positional length, not stress, and the only word stress is the final-syllable pitch peak (p. 84).
4403.quote: [p. 84] Обязательным, стабильным для всех типов словоформ является повышение ЧОТ в конце словоформы, что позволяет рассматривать финально-слоговой высотный пик как определяющий компонент кумандинского словесного ударения, факультативно сопровождающийся дополнительными компонентами длительности и интенсивности. 4403.exq_: p. 84: 'подвижное — всякий раз при наращении аффиксов перемещающееся (за некоторыми исключениями) на последний слог'; p. 79 (reporting Baskakov 1972: 38): 'фиксированное, как правило, на последнем слоге слова'. The hedge is mild ('with some exceptions', 'as a rule') and the exceptions are not named…
4403.tone: Not a tone language. Seljutina calls Kumandin word stress 'musical' (музыкальное) because its obligatory component is an F0 rise ending in a pitch peak on the final-syllable vowel (pp. 83-84: 'постепенно восходящее движение основного тона с тоновым пиком на гласном конечного слога'), with duration and intensity optional; Baskakov had called it expiratory (p. 79). This is a claim about the phonetic correlate of a fixed-position word stress, not a tonal or pitch-accent system.

For B (Northern Rengma) he gives two lexical tone minimal pairs, both on the final syllable: (i) ayi 'hail' (last syllable on a high note) vs ayi 'earth' (on a low note), p. 246 fn. 1 -- ayi is listed as the B word for 'hail' on p. 245 ('hail (legweng, A; ayi, B; awe, C)') and the footnoted form is that of 'the Tesophenyu group', i.e. Mills' Northern group = the language-B villages; (ii) mehe 'bad' (final e low) vs mehe 'good' (final e high), p. 290 fn. 1, repeated in the comparative vocabulary p. 309, B column: kemehe (final e high) 'good' / kemehe (final e low) 'bad'. Tone remarks for A: pronoun a 'I' (on low note) vs a 'he' (on high note), p. 295; conditional zolo 'if he says' with 'the final o... on a higher note than in the imperative termination', p. 301 fn. 1; haduki 'the day after to-morrow' (the u on a low note) vs haduki 'on the third day' (the u on a high note), p. 304. Intonation: negative questions use the ordinary negative verb, 'the tone of voice indicating the question', p. 303. A whole-book search for stress/accent/emphasis finds no statement on word stress or accent for any of the three languages; 'stress' occurs only non-linguistically (p. 50, 'one of the great stresses of the family complex').

4406.dloc: Ch. 8 '声调的中和与高低律': §8.1.5 pp. 228-229 and chapter scope statement §8 p. 219.
4406.prule: No stress rule stated. Northern Tujia has four lexical tones 53/44/24/21; in disyllabic words the final syllable's tone neutralizes to a level tone (44/33) and the word contour is the initial syllable's tone extended (fn. 79). The source never uses 重音/stress; it explicitly denies that the word-final syllable is weaker in intensity or shorter in duration than a normal syllable, and says that any weakened syllables are word-initial or word-medial (prefix-like, Jingpo/Dulong type).

4406.quote: [p. 219, §8.1.1] 北部土家语有四个声调，故双音节的连调模式存在16种可能性。 [p. 228, §8.1.4] 在图上，我们看到，在收尾音节的位置上，高降调53、次高平调44、低升调24和低降调21的差异消失了，都变成了一个平调。我们说，在收尾音节的位置上，土家语的声调达到了一个混沌的状态。我们将这种混沌状态称为声调的中和状态。 §8.1.5 声调中和状态不是轻声 声调的这种中和状态和一般的轻声（如普通话的）有性质的不同，主要有以下几点：1. 轻声指音节的音强比正常音节弱，音长比正常音节短，音色比正常音节更为含混。在听感上，土家语双音词的收尾音节的音强不见得弱，音长不见得短。这是声调中和与轻声最根本的差异。 [...] 3. 如果说土家语有轻声的话，那么这个轻声不是出现在收尾音节，而是分布在起首音节或多音节词的中间的音节，类似于景颇语、独龙语等语言的弱化音节（戴庆厦：1984；戴庆厦、刘菊黄：1987；孙宏开：1991）。土家语的这种弱化音节不宜处理为轻声。 [fn. 79, p. 229] 也许，土家语声调中和现象有与吴语上海话变调一致的地方：后一音节的调型变得不重要，整个双音节词的调型就是起首音节调型的扩展。参看许宝华、汤珍珠（1988）、徐云扬（1988）。

4406.exq_: 如果说土家语有轻声的话，那么这个轻声不是出现在收尾音节，而是分布在起首音节或多音节词的中间的音节 [...] 土家语的这种弱化音节不宜处理为轻声。
4406.tone: Four tones 53 (高降), 44 (次高平), 24 (低升), 21 (低降) in the Northern dialect (§8.1.1 p. 219: 北部土家语有四个声调). Disyllabic sandhi: the final syllable's tone contrast is lost, it surfaces as a level tone (声调的中和状态, pp. 227-228); the neutralized final does not trigger sandhi on the preceding syllable, unlike Mandarin 轻声 (point 2, p. 229). Zhang argues at length (§8.1.5) that this neutralization is NOT 轻声/weak syllable: the final syllable is not perceptibly weaker or shorter. Stress/accent (重音, 重读, stress, accent) never appears in the 493 scanned pages (a full-text search: the only 音强 hits are the two §8.1.5 lines quoted).

tn.quote: 2.1 Le système tonal. Le dagara a un système à deux tons: un ton haut /´/ et un ton bas /`/, puis un downstep [P.-A. Somé 1982], dont la réalisation est provoquée par l'abaissement d'un ton haut par un ton bas réalisé ou flottant (voir sur ce point Stewart [1983]). Il peut être actualisé à l'intérieur ou entre les constituants. Il est représenté par le symbole /'/ indiquant le changement de niveau tonal. La distribution de ces deux tons est organisée par des règles de polarité tonale que l'on retrouve dans les langues voltaïques
tn.translation: 2.1 The tonal system. Dagara has a two-tone system: a high tone /´/ and a low tone /`/, plus a downstep [P.-A. Somé 1982], whose realisation is triggered by the lowering of a high tone by a realised or floating low tone (see Stewart [1983] on this point). It can be actualised inside or between constituents. It is represented by the symbol /'/ indicating the change of tonal level. The distribution of these two tones is organised by rules of tonal polarity found in the Voltaic languages
tn.cite: Somé, Penou-Achille. 2001. Tout ton flottant bas autorise-t-il la propagation du ton haut précédent en Dagara-Wule? Studies in African Linguistics 30(2): 195-236.
tn.note: Two level tones (H, L) plus downstep after a realised or floating L; the morpheme, not the syllable, bears tone (no HL/LH on -VV-). Word-initial accent is in Somé 1982 §5-6, not this paper.

Vowel length is distinctive (§3.1.1.3 'L’allongement vocalique', pp. 50-51: 'En nʋnɩ, il existe bel et bien des voyelles longues et des voyelles brèves', verb pairs sʋ̃̀ 'tresser'/sʋ̃̀ʋ̃̀ 'gronder', vì 'mouiller'/vìì 'balancer', lù 'marteler'/lùù 'fer'; in nominals the word-final CVV arises from base vowel + class-suffix vowel under ATR harmony) and is not linked to any prominence.

4414.tone: Sec. 2.3 (p. 10): 'the syllable in Dinka is the unit of tone placement. Every syllable carries one and only one tone.' On stress the same book says only that each phonological word has one and only one stress, that stress is 'neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis', and that its conditioning factors 'have not been studied'; the stress marks in (5) sit on the lexical head of each two-word citation phrase (verb in aca 'yät, noun in 'mony dït, 'yök lac), not in a fixed linear position. For a nort2815 dialect proper, Blum 2023 ch. 5 (Ngok of the Padang cluster = Ngok-Sobat ngok1245) describes four tones L/H/HL/LH plus three vowel lengths and two voice qualities and never mentions stress outside its reference list. Later instrumental work on other Dinka lects finds no acoustic support for stress (Remijsen & Manyang 2009: 119 fn. 5, Luanyjang) and van Urk & Chong 2025 write that 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'; a 2025 Dataverse dataset by Blum, Goncalves Freitas, Jok & Remijsen tests for syllable stress in Dinka but has no published result.

4418.tone: Slave is a tone language with lexical (and grammatical) high tone; stress is not distinctive (Rice 1989: 46). Hare verbs show a tone shift: lexical stem high tone surfaces on the prestem vowel with low tone on the stem (Rice 1989 ch. 8; Rice 1990 sec. 3.3), while in nouns and postpositions the stem high tone stays on the stem (Rice 1990: 230). The prominence is independent of pitch: Rice 1987 fn. 5: 'I am not sure just what the phonetic correlate of what I am calling intensity is. It is definitely not pitch, as pitch as clearly discernible as tone in Hare. It appears to have to do with intensity and perhaps duration.' Rice 1987 (pp. 8-9) states the intensity difference for low-tone syllables: 'In these verbs, the prestem syllable is phonetically more intense or stronger than the stem syllable is'; in nouns and postpositions 'the vowel of the stem is of greater intensity than the vowel of the prestem syllable when both are low tone'. A prefix vowel bearing lexical high tone gains extra intensity in all dialects (Rice 1989: 46, excerpt grade).

variants.name: Slave (Dene) dialect complex as a whole (Rice 1989); the positional statement concerns the Hare dialect (hare1244)
variants.prule: Stress is not distinctive in Slave, a two-tone (high/low) language. In the Hare dialect there are predictable 'stress-like properties': what might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a VERB and on the STEM vowel of a NOUN; intensity is the primary phonetic correlate (details deferred to chapter 8, the tone chapter). In prefixes in all dialects, a vowel with lexical high tone on which a high tone falls has extra stress, i.e. is more intense; e.g. the 1sg and 3sg perfective differ only by tone placement, and a high tone landing on an already high-toned vowel gives it prominent stress.
variants.quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. See chapter 8. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense. ... In the perfective, the first and third person singular forms differ only by tone placement. Where the high tone falls on a vowel already bearing a high tone, as in the first person singular perfective form, this vowel retains its tone and receives prominent stress.

4419.dq: Word stress is assigned after CG applies, with no consideration of whether a given syllable has or has not been altered by CG. Whereas CG affects alternate syllables, as explained below, resembling Yupik prosody in this respect, word stress is assigned individually to syllables practically regardless of what precedes or follows.
4419.heavy: 'the non-final closed syllables and all long vowels—including diphthongs and vowel clusters, which are phonetically long—receive stress'; 'A long consonant, like a consonant cluster, has the effect of closing the preceding syllable'. So heavy = CVV/diphthong/vowel cluster anywhere, and CVC (cluster- or geminate-closed) only when non-final; a word-final closed syllable is not heavy by closure alone.
4419.dflt: None: a word of light syllables only is 'equally stressless' (iřítuq gets its stress only because CG lengthens t and closes the second syllable); no fallback position is stated.
4419.prule: Quantity-driven, non-culminative word stress: every heavy syllable is stressed, where heavy = any non-final closed syllable (closed by a consonant cluster or a long/geminate consonant, underlying or created by Consonant Gradation) and any syllable with a phonetically long nucleus (long vowel aa/ii/uu, diphthong ai/au, or vowel cluster iu/ui/ia/ua) in any position; light (short open) syllables are unstressed, and a word whose syllables are all light is 'equally stressless'. Long vowels and diphthongs are stressed over their whole quantity; vowel clusters carry stress on their second member except word-finally (úi, niγiřúaq). Stress is assigned syllable by syllable after Consonant Gradation, with no fixed edge, no rhythm and no designated primary peak.
4419.srule: Not mentioned in Kaplan 1985 (section 2, pp. 193-194; whole article pp. 191-210): the stresses of a word are not ranked; every heavy syllable is stressed equally (Inúktuyúuq) and an all-light word is 'equally stressless'.

4423.prule: One culminative word stress, never final, always on the first or second syllable. Disyllables: stress on the first syllable regardless of lexical tone or vowel length. Words of three or more syllables: stress on the second syllable by default (phonologically toneless words, e.g. [iˈpuːrɛi] 'dress', [naˈqasɨrɛi] 'scorpion', [iːˈbɨxi] 'breathes', [taːˈtasəi] 'splits'), but on the first syllable when that syllable carries the lexical H tone ([ˈúːʎiɟɨ] 'his maternal grandmother'). Position is thus set by word size plus lexical tone, not by weight (JIPA 2021, the author's later refereed description). The earlier AMP 9 conference paper (same author, same speakers, PDF dated March 2021) formulated the same surface facts as 'stress on the first heavy syllable (long vowel, consonant or glide coda), otherwise on the second', NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT, with heavy-initial second-stressed words treated as lexical-L exceptions (*ALIGN(HEAD/LOW)); JIPA drops weight and treats those words as regular toneless/second-H cases.

4423.tone: JIPA 2021: 'a tonal language with a single phonological tone: the high tone H' (privative /H/), 'low tonal density' (not all morphemes specified), H culminative (at most once per phonological word), H 'only occurs in the first two syllables of a root and in some suffixes'; 'a high pitch is also a correlate of stress in toneless words, but stress and high pitch could not coincide when lexical H is present' (in H-final disyllables stress stays initial, identified by vowel quality, intensity and native-speaker judgment). AMP 9 2021 analyses the same pitch facts as a privative /L/ on the long first vowel of L.H disyllables, with stress cued by an intonational H* that docks on the stressed syllable unless a lexical L blocks it (constraint *ALIGN(HEAD/LOW)); 1200-entry lexical base, F0 on 265 H.L and 427 L.H disyllabic tokens. Both analyses agree on the surface: a single non-final word stress in the first or second syllable, initial in disyllables, and in longer words on the first syllable only when it carries the pitch prominence (JIPA: lexical H; AMP: weight, minus L-toned exceptions). Bascom 1982: 272 (SIL grammar sketch, in the copy consulted) had claimed 'Stress is noncontrastive. It is freely fluctuation in many words.' with two tones (high marked, low unmarked); Bascom 1959 'Tonomechanics' (paywalled) is the equipollent H/L source; Kim 1997 (WCCFL 15, not located) derived tone from metrical stress.

4426.dq: In ConQ, word-level main stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on the initial syllable, and tertiary stresses on alternating syllables preceding the penult. [p.196] ... These rules provide a working mechanism for the assignment of word-level stress in ConQ. [p.207] ... 4426.heavy: Syllables containing long vowels (written as geminates) are heavy = branching nucleus; 'aw, ay, uy and iy represent diphthongs, which behave like the long vowels (ie. branching nuclei) for the purposes of stress assignment'; 'All other syllables, with few exceptions -to be discussed- are light' (p.195). In three-syllable words only, 'Penults with branching rimes in three-syllable words are counted as heavy' (closed syllables; pp.205, 207). Long vowels may not occur in closed syllables (p.194).
4426.dflt: penultimate main stress (word-level); in all-light trisyllables penult with an optional initial variant; disyllables initial = penult
4426.prule: Word-level main stress on the penultimate syllable by default, with quantity sensitivity: in words of four or more syllables a word-final long vowel or diphthong following a light penult 'usually' (formalised as optionally) takes main stress, but the penult always wins when the last two syllables are both heavy; disyllables are always initial(=penult)-stressed regardless of weight; in trisyllables a heavy penult (long vowel or closed syllable) is always main-stressed, a light penult after a heavy initial never is (initial stress), a heavy final after two light syllables optionally takes main stress, and all-light trisyllables vary between penultimate and initial stress.
4426.srule: Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable; weaker (tertiary) stresses on alternating syllables preceding the penult, footed right-to-left in binary quantity-sensitive left-dominant feet (all-light words: 1010, 10010, 101010, 1001010 with main stress on the penult); every long vowel or diphthong not bearing main stress also carries secondary stress ('length consistently attracts secondary stress').

4428.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, always; quantity-insensitive. Basic words are disyllabic couplets, so stress is root-initial in simple words, but the rule is stated for the word of any length (rule (5) applies to any word-level category) and is shown holding in 3-4 syllable derived verbs, compounds and -kuei plurals.
4428.srule: None: one stressed syllable per word ('Hay una sola sílaba tónica', Gittlen & Gittlen 2008: 83; 'En mixteco la sílaba más fuerte siempre es la penúltima', p. 6). Secondary stress is not mentioned in Gittlen 2016 (sec. 1.2 pp. 6-9, sec. 2.1(c) p. 15) or Gittlen & Marlett 1985 (pp. 176-178, 186-190), which describe only the penultimate (primary) stress; 1985 p. 188: compounds keep a single penultimate stress.

tn.quote: En el mixteco del norte de Tlaxiaco, algunas palabras se pronuncian casi iguales; solamente el nivel de la voz hace la diferencia. El nivel, que se llama “tono”, puede ser alto (agudo), bajo (grave) o medio. Generalmente, no habrá confusión entre palabras que difieren solamente en el tono porque la oración o contexto en que se usan ayuda a distinguirlas. A pesar de la distinción que el tono pueda hacer entre dos o más palabras, en esta variante del mixteco, no se está utilizando ningún símbolo especial para marcar el tono. ndee costar / ndee salir / ndee bajar / ndee hasta …
tn.translation: In Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec some words are pronounced almost the same; only the level of the voice makes the difference. The level, called 'tone', can be high (acute), low (grave) or mid. Generally there is no confusion between words that differ only in tone because the sentence or context in which they are used helps distinguish them. Despite the distinction tone can make between two or more words, in this variety of Mixtec no special symbol is being used to mark tone. ndee 'cost' / ndee 'go out' / ndee 'go down' / ndee 'until' ...

tn.note: Three level tones, high, mid and low, distinguish otherwise identical words; tone is not written; a higher tone marks continuative aspect; stress is separate and always penultimate.
